For the printed film, we additionally scaled up production to ~1 kg using a new method that maintained high-temperature dissolution and precipitation steps using a jacketed vessel. With this material, we were able to create a cast film from PE to characterize mechanical and optical properties in collaboration with Amcor, thereby ensuring suitability of the resin for reuse in packaging applications (Figure 3.5.2). Properties of the cast were compared to two virgin films provided by Amcor. Visual methods to identify impurities (e.g., due to the formation of gels during the precipitation process) found the STRAP samples close to commercial standards. We analyzed optical properties including the clarity, haze %, and yellowness index, with the PE produced by the jacketed dissolution vessel yielding values most similar to the control films. Finally, mechanical properties (and specifically tensile properties, including the Young’s modulus, stress at break, force at break, and elongation at break) were again compared to the controls. Values from the jacketed dissolution approach were again found to be most similar to the virgin materials. Together, these experiments (including characterization of the nylon film) met Milestone 3.5.2: Characterize recovered polymer properties – including solution and melt rheological properties - to ensure suitability for reuse and G/NG Milestone 3.5.3: Design solvents systems and processing temperatures to recover >90 wt% of two high-volume commercial flexible films identified using STRAP technology and demonstrate that recovered resins have properties similar to virgin resins. Figure 3.5.2: Schematic showing the printed film (at left) studied in Task 3.5. A new approach using a jacketed dissolution tank (at middle) was developed to generate ~1 kg of STRAP pe with similar wt % recovery as smaller-scale STRAP experiments. These materials were used to extrude a cast a film (at right), which had comparable optical and mechanical properties to control films. These experiments, combined with similar experiments on a second flexible film, met G/NG Milestone 3.5.3. Finally, results in Task 4.5: Development of STRAP process for high-quality post- consumer waste films extended the successes from Task 3.5 to a high-quality post- consumer waste feedstock consisting of plastic shrink wrap that was sourced from a materials recovery facility. The shrink wrap consisted primarily of LLDPE and LDPE. We extracted PE by dissolution in xylene and successfully removed paper and adhesives using a filtration vessel with a 100 μm filter. Films created from this PE were compared to virgin LLDPE and a pellet of typical post-consumer recycled material obtained after mechanical recycling (Figure 3.5.3). The PE recovered from STRAP had optical very similar to virgin PE, which was a substantial improvement upon mechanically recycled resins. This result indicates the capability to apply STRAP to post-consumer shrink wrap films, meeting Milestone 4.5.1: Design solvent compositions and processing temperatures for the selective dissolution of the polymer components of rigid and flexible PCW films identified by industrial partners. We further scaled up this process to ~1 kg using the jacketed dissolution vessel approach to generate sufficient material for extrusion and film casting (Figure 3.5.3).
